title: Chernobyl: The Night Reactor Four Exploded
alt_titles: How Chernobyl Really Happened, Minute by Minute
Chernobyl: The Test That Went Wrong
Chernobyl: The Disaster the Soviet Union Tried to Hide
description_summary: At 1.23am on 26 April 1986, Reactor Number Four at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant exploded during a safety test. This is the story of how the test went wrong, how the Soviet state stayed silent until Sweden detected the radiation, and why the official explanation changed years later.

unverified.reason: Sources give 45,000 to 49,000; the script uses 'around forty five thousand'.
Long-term estimates vary widely; the script presents the Chernobyl Forum projection and says others are higher.
Some sources say little reached the core; the script says it is debated.

scenes.narration: It was the early hours of Saturday the twenty sixth of April 1986. At the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine, engineers were running a safety test on Reactor Number Four. They had been waiting hours to start it. At twenty three minutes past one, they pressed the emergency shutdown button. Seconds later, the reactor exploded.

The blast tore open the reactor building and threw burning debris across the site. Some of the reactor's fuel and graphite was hurled out of the building. Two workers died that night. Over the following days, radioactive material drifted across Ukraine, Belarus, Russia and much of Europe. The release would go on for days. It was the worst accident in the history of nuclear power.

shots.caption: The damaged Unit 4 reactor
Caesium-137 contamination around Chernobyl, mapped in 1996

scenes.narration: This is the story of Chernobyl. It covers how a routine test went wrong. It shows how the Soviet state tried to keep it quiet, and how the official explanation changed years later. It begins with the reactor itself.

shots.file: File:Transmission towers for the transfer of electricity frame the damaged unit 4 reactor at Chernobyl (02710143).jpg

scenes.narration: The Chernobyl plant stood near the new town of Pripyat, built for its workers and their families. Around forty five thousand people lived there in 1986. The town had schools, shops, a hospital and a fairground. The plant had four working reactors. Each one could produce a thousand megawatts of electricity.

shots.caption: The Chernobyl nuclear power plant
Pripyat, the town built for the plant's workers

scenes.narration: They were a Soviet design called the RBMK. Uranium fuel sat in channels inside a huge block of graphite, cooled by water. The design had a dangerous quirk, which made it hard to control at low power. In some conditions, steam bubbles in the cooling water made the reaction speed up instead of slowing down.

shots.caption: A model of the inside of Unit 4
How an RBMK reactor works

scenes.narration: The test on Unit Four was meant to fix a safety gap. If the plant lost power, the cooling pumps would stop until backup diesel generators started. Engineers wanted to know if the spinning turbines could keep the pumps running in between. An earlier test, in 1985, had failed.

shots.file: File:Turbine Hall of Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant Unit 4 (9032364808).jpg
shots.caption: The turbine hall of Unit 4

scenes.narration: The test was due on the afternoon of the twenty fifth. But at two o'clock, the grid controller in Kyiv asked for a delay. Electricity was needed for the evening rush. The power reduction did not resume until eleven at night, and a new shift took over at midnight.

card.label: The delay before the test went ahead
card.note: From the afternoon to the night shift

scenes.narration: The night shift was led by shift supervisor Aleksandr Akimov. At the controls was senior reactor engineer Leonid Toptunov, aged twenty five. Directing the test was the deputy chief engineer, Anatoly Dyatlov. He was there to see the test through to the end.

As they lowered the power, it suddenly fell much further than planned, to almost nothing. To bring it back up, operators pulled out most of the control rods that slow the reaction. Automatic safety systems had been switched off for the test. The reactor was now in a very unstable state.

At four seconds past one twenty three, the test began. The turbine was cut off and the pumps slowed. More steam formed in the core, and power began to climb. At one twenty three and forty seconds, the operators pressed the emergency shutdown button, known as AZ five.

The control rods should have stopped the reaction. Instead, because of a flaw in their design, they briefly made it worse as they went in. Power surged far beyond the reactor's limits. A steam explosion followed, then a second, more powerful blast two or three seconds later.

The blasts lifted the reactor's thousand tonne lid and threw hot graphite and fuel across the site. Fires broke out on the roof of the turbine hall. Firefighters led by Lieutenant Volodymyr Pravyk were among the first to arrive. They put out the roof fires within a few hours.

shots.caption: The Unit 4 reactor building at Chernobyl

shots.file: File:The ventilation stack of the damaged unit 4 reactor at Chernobyl (02710157).jpg
shots.caption: The ventilation stack beside the damaged Unit 4

scenes.narration: Many of the first responders had received huge doses of radiation. Pravyk died about two weeks later. In all, acute radiation sickness was confirmed in one hundred and thirty four people. Twenty eight of them died within a few months, including six firemen.

card.label: People confirmed with acute radiation sickness

shots.caption: A memorial to the Chernobyl firefighters

scenes.narration: Pripyat was not evacuated that night. The order came early on Sunday the twenty seventh. Buses arrived from two o'clock that afternoon, about thirty six hours after the explosion. Residents were told to pack for about three days.

card.text: Buses arrive for every apartment block

shots.caption: Pripyat's empty apartment blocks, 2009

scenes.narration: They never came back. About forty five thousand people left Pripyat that day. Ten days after the accident, the evacuation zone was widened to thirty kilometres around the plant. By the middle of May, around one hundred and sixteen thousand people had been moved.

card.label: People evacuated by mid-May 1986
card.note: From within 30 km of the plant

shots.caption: Pripyat today, abandoned since 1986

scenes.narration: Moscow said nothing in public. Then, on the morning of Monday the twenty eighth, radiation alarms went off at the Forsmark nuclear plant in Sweden. They had been set off by contamination on a worker's shoes. Raised readings were soon found elsewhere in Sweden, and in Finland. The radiation had not come from Forsmark. It had blown in on winds from the east. Experts traced it by studying the weather.

shots.caption: The Forsmark nuclear plant in Sweden

scenes.narration: That evening, Soviet television's main news programme finally mentioned the accident. The item lasted about twenty seconds. It said only that the effects of the accident were being dealt with. It gave no details of the danger. It came more than two and a half days after the explosion.

shots.caption: Soviet television's evening news

card.label: The first Soviet TV report, 28 April
card.note: Two and a half days after the explosion

scenes.narration: Inside the wrecked reactor, the graphite kept burning, releasing radiation as it did. Helicopters dropped more than five thousand tonnes of sand, clay, lead and boron onto it. How much reached the core is still debated. The fire was finally out by the tenth of May.

card.label: Of sand, clay, lead and boron dropped

scenes.narration: The clean-up workers became known as liquidators. Around two hundred thousand took part in 1986 and 1987, and over six hundred thousand in later years. About twenty thousand of them received high doses. Some of them cleared radioactive debris from the roofs next to the ruined reactor.

shots.caption: Medals awarded to Chernobyl 'liquidators'
A memorial to the liquidators in Slavutych

card.label: 'Liquidators' who took part in the clean-up

scenes.narration: Within seven months, workers had built a huge concrete and steel shelter over the ruined reactor. It became known as the sarcophagus. It was finished by the end of 1986, and the plant's other reactors kept running for years afterwards.

shots.caption: A model of the 1986 'sarcophagus'

card.text: The sarcophagus is built in about seven months

shots.caption: The sarcophagus over Unit 4

scenes.narration: In August 1986, Soviet experts presented their findings to the International Atomic Energy Agency. The blame fell on the operators, who were said to have broken the rules. The official verdict was human error. In July 1987, six men went on trial in the town of Chernobyl itself. The plant's director and Anatoly Dyatlov were each sentenced to ten years.

card.label: Sentence for the plant director and for Dyatlov

scenes.narration: But the story changed. A Soviet commission in 1991 found that operators had not broken rules that had never been written down. In 1992, a new international report shifted the main cause to the reactor's design: its steam problem and the faulty control rods. Operators had never been warned about these dangers.

card.text: The design was the main cause

scenes.narration: The 1992 report still called some of the operators' actions ill judged. Both the reactor and the way it was run had played a part. Dyatlov was released early in 1990 because of ill health. He died in 1995.

card.title: What went wrong
items: Control rods that made it worse

scenes.narration: The long-term toll is still argued over. Among people exposed as children, thousands developed thyroid cancer, which is usually treatable. A 2005 study led by United Nations agencies projected up to four thousand eventual deaths among the most exposed. Other estimates are far higher.

card.label: Projected eventual deaths among the most exposed

shots.caption: A warning sign in the exclusion zone

scenes.narration: About three hundred and fifty thousand people were eventually resettled. An exclusion zone of around two thousand six hundred square kilometres still surrounds the plant. Inside it, Pripyat stands empty, its fairground Ferris wheel now one of the best-known symbols of the disaster.

shots.caption: The Ferris wheel in Pripyat's fairground
Pripyat's abandoned fairground

scenes.narration: The sarcophagus was only ever meant to be temporary. In November 2016, a giant steel arch called the New Safe Confinement was slid over it on rails. It had been built beside the reactor, then moved into position. It is one hundred and ten metres high and weighs thirty six thousand tonnes.

shots.caption: The arch before it was slid into place, August 2016
The New Safe Confinement over Unit 4

card.label: Weight of the New Safe Confinement

scenes.narration: Twenty years after the accident, Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader in 1986, looked back on it. He wrote that Chernobyl, even more than his own reforms, was perhaps the real cause of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

shots.caption: Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader at the time

card.text: Perhaps the real cause of the Soviet collapse

shots.caption: The finished arch, October 2017

scenes.narration: Chernobyl was not caused by one mistake. A flawed reactor, a delayed and badly run test, and a system that hid problems all played their part. Its lessons changed how reactors are designed and run around the world. Sources and image credits are in the description.
